children: Bitcoin ETF outflows have reached $2.347 billion across the first two completed November trading weeks, leaving a persistent hole in one of the market’s most closely watched sources of demand.

BNC’s calculations from Farside Investors’ fund-flow table show $1.0653 billion leaving U.S. spot Bitcoin funds during November 9–13, following $1.2817 billion in the preceding week. BlackRock’s IBIT recorded withdrawals on every session in both weeks and on October 30, extending its losing streak to 11 trading days.

The figures describe net investor flows through the products. They do not mean BlackRock’s corporate treasury has decided to sell its own Bitcoin holdings, or establish that every departing investor has abandoned cryptocurrency altogether.
Bitcoin ETF outflows remain concentrated in IBIT

IBIT accounted for $908.4 million of the latest week’s net withdrawals, about 85% of the industry total. Its November withdrawals through Friday reached $2.118 billion, approximately 90% of the combined net outflow across the funds.

Concentration matters when interpreting the headline. One very large product can drive the aggregate even while some competing funds attract money. An industry total does not show that every provider or customer group is moving in the same direction.

Friday’s $185.4 million net withdrawal was smaller than Thursday’s $284.1 million. But a less negative session remains a negative session. It is evidence that the pace changed, rather than confirmation that demand has recovered.

The industry’s losing run is shorter than IBIT’s: seven sessions, beginning November 5. On November 4, the combined funds attracted $74.6 million even as IBIT lost money. That is a concrete example of why a fund-specific streak and an industry-wide streak should not be used interchangeably. The totals here use the table as checked on November 15; automated flow datasets can subsequently be revised.

children: A large fund is still a large fund
The iShares product page reported IBIT net assets of approximately $54.13 billion as of November 13. Its net asset value was $39.00 per share, while its closing market price was $38.94.

Those figures put the withdrawals beside a substantial remaining investor base. They also illustrate why assets under management and fund flows should not be treated as interchangeable: assets can shrink because Bitcoin falls, because investors redeem shares, or through a combination of both.

Likewise, trading volume in ETF shares is not automatically a net inflow. Shares can change hands between buyers and sellers on an exchange without the product receiving an equivalent amount of new capital. That distinction becomes particularly useful during volatile sessions.

Reading the market therefore requires separate questions: how much exposure investors retain, how much new money enters or leaves, and how the underlying asset is priced. One dramatic number cannot answer all three.
BlackRock’s longer-term argument faces a near-term test

BlackRock has previously argued that weak flows do not necessarily overturn Bitcoin’s long-term investment case. In an earlier research paper using data through mid-2026, its digital-assets team described the pullback’s pressures as “cyclical flow dynamics.”

The paper, co-authored by Robert Mitchnick, Will Su and Alice Wang, separated episodes of leveraged selling and slowing institutional demand from its case for Bitcoin as a longer-term portfolio diversifier. It also discussed competition for capital from AI-themed investments.

That research predates the November withdrawals. It should be read as the manager’s investment framework, not a fresh explanation of this particular week. BlackRock also sponsors IBIT, giving readers a reason to distinguish its commercial perspective from the independently tabulated flows.

The tension is useful rather than contradictory. A long-term thesis can remain intact in an investor’s view while near-term allocations decline. The practical test is whether that conviction eventually translates into renewed purchases.

The ETF figures cannot isolate inflation, sentiment or any other single cause of redemptions. Nor do they reveal whether investors are reducing leverage, changing vehicles, raising cash or making a permanent allocation decision. Those explanations require evidence beyond the daily totals.
What would signal a more durable improvement?

The next useful development would be sustained net buying across several sessions, ideally involving more than one fund. A single positive day could interrupt a streak without changing the wider demand picture.

It would also help to compare fund flows with spot trading and derivatives positioning over matching dates. A weekend Bitcoin move takes place while U.S. fund shares are not in their normal trading session; it should not be described as a new daily ETF-flow reading.

For now, the completed-week data show repeated withdrawals from a major access route into Bitcoin. The important question for the next trading week is whether that drain slows convincingly—and whether buyers return in sufficient size to turn stabilisation into fresh demand.

title: Bitcoin ETFs Shed $2.35 Billion in Two Weeks as BlackRock’s Outflow Streak Hits 11
